x-m-e6-01.title: Checking Minseo's fraction division
x-m-e6-01.goal: Find the wrong line in a fraction division solution, check by turning it into multiplication that the answer is wrong, and correct it.
x-m-e6-01.material: Minseo calculated 3/4 ÷ 2/3 (three fourths divided by two thirds), but the teacher said, “Your answer is different.” Below is Minseo's solution. Read fractions in words, like “three fourths.”
x-m-e6-01.thinking.0: Find where the error is in the solution
x-m-e6-01.thinking.1: Check the answer using the relationship between multiplication and division
x-m-e6-01.thinking.2: Explain the cause of the error in words
x-m-e6-01.prereq.0: Multiplying fractions, reducing fractions, and writing improper fractions as mixed numbers (Grade 5 level)
x-m-e6-01.prereq.1: Division and multiplication are opposite operations
x-m-e6-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Minseo's solution.
x-m-e6-01.s.s1.hint.0: Follow how each line came from the line right before it.
x-m-e6-01.s.s1.hint.1: Check which numbers were changed, and whether two numbers were changed.
x-m-e6-01.s.s1.line.1: Swap the numerator and denominator of the divisor 2/3 and write 3/2.
x-m-e6-01.s.s1.line.2: Also swap the numerator and denominator of the dividend 3/4 and write 4/3.
x-m-e6-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first wrong place. Only the divisor 2/3 should be flipped; the dividend 3/4 should stay as it is. The calculation in line 4 just followed line 3.
x-m-e6-01.s.s2.prompt: Which is a good way to check that Minseo's answer 2 is wrong?
x-m-e6-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what “quotient × divisor” should equal.
x-m-e6-01.s.s2.o.a: The answer 2 is a whole number and looks neat, so it is probably right
x-m-e6-01.s.s2.r.a: An answer looking neat is not evidence that it is right. You need to check a division answer by calculating.
x-m-e6-01.s.s2.explain: The quotient times the divisor should equal the dividend. 2 × 2/3 = 4/3, which is not 3/4, so 2 is a wrong answer.
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.prompt: Write the correct answer to 3/4 ÷ 2/3, and explain in one or two sentences what Minseo changed wrongly and how.
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write the corrected solution in one line.
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.hint.1: Put “which number you change” into your words.
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check your answer by multiplying, rather than just comparing it with 2?
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why “changing the dividend too” is a problem?
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.model.0: 3/4 × 3/2 = 9/8 = 1 1/8. Only the divisor 2/3 gets changed to 3/2, but Minseo changed 3/4 too, so it was wrong.
x-m-e6-01.s.s3.model.1: Only the divisor is flipped, so it becomes 3/4 × 3/2 and the answer is 9/8, that is, 1 and 1/8. Minseo flipped the first number as well.

x-m-e6-02.title: Dividing 12 made it bigger
x-m-e6-02.goal: Check, by building your own divisions that fit the conditions, that dividing a whole number by a fraction less than 1 gives a quotient bigger than the starting number, and explain why.
x-m-e6-02.material: Jia said, “Dividing makes numbers smaller!” Let's divide 12 by some fractions to check whether this is true.
x-m-e6-02.thinking.0: Predict how big the result of a division will be
x-m-e6-02.thinking.1: Make examples that meet several conditions at once
x-m-e6-02.prereq.0: The relationship between fractions and whole numbers; the meaning of a fraction that cannot be reduced any further (a fraction in lowest terms)
x-m-e6-02.prereq.1: Experience of thinking of division as “how many times it fits inside”
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.prompt: How does the quotient of 12 divided by 1/3 (one third) compare with 12?
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.hint.0: First picture how many times 1/3 fits inside 1.
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.hint.1: Then how many times will it fit inside 12?
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.o.a: It gets smaller than 12. Dividing always makes numbers smaller
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.r.a: You are using your experience of dividing whole numbers for fractions as it is. Also look at what kind of number the divisor is.
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.o.b: It gets bigger than 12. 1/3 fits inside 12 more than 12 times
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.r.b: You interpreted division as “how many times it fits inside.”
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.o.c: It is the same as 12. The numerator is 1, so the size of the number doesn't change
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.r.c: You only looked at the numerator being 1. Think again about what the division is asking.
x-m-e6-02.s.s1.explain: 1/3 is less than 1, so 1/3 fits inside 12 thirty-six times. So 12 ÷ 1/3 = 36, which is bigger than 12.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to divide 12 by a proper fraction a/b (numerator a, denominator b). Make 3 different fractions that cannot be reduced any further, with a quotient that is a whole number and at most 60.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.hint.0: First look at what numbers can be the numerator, in relation to 12.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a numerator, then change the denominator and check whether the quotient is a whole number and at most 60.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerator and denominator are whole numbers.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerator and denominator must be whole numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a proper fraction (the numerator is smaller than the denominator).
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not a proper fraction. The numerator must be smaller than the denominator.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.ok.c3: It cannot be reduced any further.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The numerator and denominator have a common factor greater than 1, so it can be reduced.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.ok.c4: The quotient 12×b÷a is a whole number.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.fail.c4: The quotient is not a whole number.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.explain: For example, 12 ÷ 1/3 = 36, 12 ÷ 2/5 = 30, and 12 ÷ 3/4 = 16. For the quotient to be a whole number, the numerator must divide 12 evenly.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Jia's statement “Dividing makes numbers smaller” did not hold in the divisions you made above. Explain why, focusing on the divisor.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Look at how the fraction you made compares with 1.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about how many times that fraction fits inside 12.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: Because the divisor is less than 1, ...
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain using a fraction you made as an example?
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you also think about what happens when “the divisor is greater than 1”?
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.model.0: Because the divisor is a fraction less than 1, the number of times it fits inside 12 is more than 12. So the quotient gets bigger.
x-m-e6-02.s.s2.because.model.1: When you divide by the proper fraction 1/2, you aren't splitting 12 in half; you are counting how many times 1/2 fits in, so you get 24, which is a bigger number.

x-m-e6-03.title: Does more concentrate mean stronger juice?
x-m-e6-03.goal: Show with a counterexample that the claim “the one with more concentrate is always stronger” does not always hold, and explain why you must compare using the ratio of concentrate to the whole.
x-m-e6-03.material: At a juice shop, two juices were made by mixing concentrate and water using the same cup. Juice A uses 3 cups of concentrate and 5 cups of water, and Juice B uses 4 cups of concentrate and 8 cups of water. Hajun said, “B has more concentrate, 4 cups, so B is stronger!” (Here, “stronger” means that when you drink the same amount, there is more concentrate in it.)
x-m-e6-03.thinking.2: Find and explain the standard (the whole) to compare against
x-m-e6-03.prereq.0: The meaning of ratio and rate (the compared quantity and the base quantity)
x-m-e6-03.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of fractions with one- and two-digit whole numbers
x-m-e6-03.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Hajun's judgment?
x-m-e6-03.s.s1.hint.0: If you drink the same amount (for example, one cup), how much concentrate is in it?
x-m-e6-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the total amounts of the two juices are the same.
x-m-e6-03.s.s1.o.a: Right. The juice with more concentrate is always stronger
x-m-e6-03.s.s1.r.a: You looked at only one thing, the amount of concentrate. Test whether the same conclusion holds when the total mixed amount is different.
x-m-e6-03.s.s1.explain: How strong a juice is depends not just on the concentrate but on how much concentrate there is compared with the whole mixture. A has 3 cups out of 8 cups in all, and B has 4 cups out of 12 cups in all.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.hint.0: B needs more concentrate, so what happens if you also put a lot of water in B?
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.hint.1: For each juice, write how much of the whole is concentrate as a division or a fraction, and compare.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of cups are whole numbers from 1 to 20.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of cups must be a whole number from 1 to 20.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.fail.c2: B's concentrate must be more than A's concentrate.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.fail.c3: A is not stronger. Compare how much concentrate there is relative to the total amount.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.prompt: You want to tell Hajun, “That's not always true.” Explain using the numbers in the example you made.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: First decide which numbers you will use as the example.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put into your words what you need to look at together with the “amount of concentrate.”
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you only look at the concentrate, ...
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In your example, do the numbers show why A is stronger?
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that “has more concentrate” and “is stronger” do not mean the same thing?
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.model.0: Don't look at the amount of concentrate only. You have to look at the ratio of concentrate to the total amount; A is 3/8 and B is 4/12, so Juice A is stronger.
x-m-e6-03.s.s2.because.model.1: B has a lot of concentrate, but a lot of water too. A is 3 cups out of 8 and B is 4 cups out of 12, so when you compare the ratios, A is stronger.

x-m-e6-04.title: Whose win rate is higher?
x-m-e6-04.goal: Know that to compare win rates, the number of wins is not enough and the total number of games is needed, and find several numbers of games that fit the conditions.
x-m-e6-04.material: In a kickball league, Class A has won 12 times so far and Class B has won 9 times. Seoyun said, “Class A won 3 more times, so Class A is better!” The win rate is the ratio of games won to all games played.
x-m-e6-04.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
x-m-e6-04.thinking.2: Find several values that meet the conditions
x-m-e6-04.prereq.0: The meaning of a rate, and writing a rate as a fraction or decimal
x-m-e6-04.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of whole numbers
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.prompt: To find out which class has the higher win rate, what do you need to know besides the number of wins? Choose the one best answer.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the wins 12 and 9 were counted against the same base.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.hint.1: Say what the “base quantity” of the win rate is.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.o.a: The results of the games when the two classes played each other
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.r.a: The results of games between the two are only a part of the whole. A win rate is figured over all the games a class has played.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.o.b: The number of students in the two classes
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.r.b: The number of students is not the base quantity for the win rate. Think about what quantity is the base for a win rate.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.o.c: The total number of games each of Class A and Class B has played
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.r.c: You saw that the number of wins has to be compared against the same base (the total number of games).
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.o.d: The number of losses of Class A and Class B
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.r.d: You saw that adding the wins and losses gives the total number of games.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.explain: A win rate compares the number of wins to the total number of games, so you need the total number of games. If you know the losses, you can also find the total number of games, so it is the same information.
x-m-e6-04.s.s1.acc.0: If you know the losses, you can add them to the wins to get the total number of games, so that is enough to find the win rate.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.prompt: Class B won 9 of its 15 games in all. Class A won 12 times. For Class A's win rate to be higher than Class B's, how many games in all could Class A have played? Find 3 possible numbers of games.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.hint.0: First write Class B's win rate as a fraction or decimal.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a total number of games, divide 12 by it, and compare with Class B's value.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.var.n: Class A's total number of games
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.ok.c1: Class A won 12 times, so the total number of games is a whole number that is at least 12.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.fail.c1: It can't be fewer than the 12 games already won. It must be a whole number.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Class A's win rate is higher than Class B's.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Class A's win rate is not higher than Class B's (9/15).
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.explain: Class B's win rate is 9/15 = 0.6. For Class A's 12/n to be greater than 0.6, n must be less than 20, so every n from 12 to 19 is possible.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain by comparing win rates why a total of 20 games does not work.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Find Class A's win rate for 20 games.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put that value side by side with Class B's win rate.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the two values you calculated are really equal?
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say the difference between “must be higher” and “is equal”?
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.model.0: If n is 20, Class A's win rate is 12/20 = 0.6 and Class B's 9/15 is also 0.6, so they are equal. It isn't higher, so it doesn't work.
x-m-e6-04.s.s2.because.model.1: With 20 games, Class A's win rate is also 60% and Class B's win rate is 60%, so they are the same. If they are equal, you can't say Class A is higher.

x-m-e6-05.title: Does a box that needs more wrapping paper hold more?
x-m-e6-05.topic: Volume and surface area of a rectangular prism
x-m-e6-05.goal: Show with a counterexample that the claim “a rectangular prism with a larger surface area has a larger volume” does not hold, and explain the reason by connecting it to shape.
x-m-e6-05.material: Jimin works wrapping rectangular boxes at a gift shop and said, “A box that takes more wrapping paper (a box with a larger surface area) holds more stuff (has a larger volume)!” Length, width, and height are in cm and are all whole numbers.
x-m-e6-05.thinking.0: Make a counterexample to a claim
x-m-e6-05.thinking.1: Compare two quantities (surface area and volume) together
x-m-e6-05.thinking.2: Explain the relationship between shape and quantity
x-m-e6-05.prereq.0: The meaning of surface area and volume of a rectangular prism and how to find them (Grade 6)
x-m-e6-05.prereq.1: Writing length, width, and height as whole numbers (cm)
x-m-e6-05.s.s1.prompt: To show that Jimin's statement is not “always” true, what kind of boxes should you look for?
x-m-e6-05.s.s1.hint.0: Remember that the word “always” can be broken by just one example.
x-m-e6-05.s.s1.hint.1: In the two boxes, the two quantities have to go in opposite directions.
x-m-e6-05.s.s1.explain: If “a larger surface area means a larger volume” were always true, there would be no such boxes. If even one pair exists, the claim is wrong.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose box P (length a, width b, height c) and box Q (length d, width e, height f) so that P has the larger surface area but P has the smaller volume, and make 2 different example pairs. All lengths are whole numbers from 1 to 20 cm.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.hint.0: Try starting with P as a very long, thin box and Q as a box whose edges are about the same length.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.hint.1: Each time you pick a box, calculate both the surface area and the volume and compare.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.ok.c1: All lengths are whole numbers from 1 to 20.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.fail.c1: All lengths must be whole numbers from 1 to 20.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.ok.c2: P has the larger surface area.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.fail.c2: P's surface area is not larger than Q's.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.fail.c3: P's volume is not smaller than Q's.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.explain: If P is 1×1×20, the surface area is 82 cm² and the volume is 20 cm³, and if Q is 3×3×3, the surface area is 54 cm² and the volume is 27 cm³. 1×2×10 (surface area 64, volume 20) and 2×3×4 (surface area 52, volume 24) also work.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Using the shapes of the boxes, explain why a box can have a larger surface area but a smaller volume.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Describe the shapes of P and Q in words (long and thin, or close to a cube).
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Look at which faces or edges count most for surface area and for volume.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain using one of the boxes you made as an example?
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart shapes where only the surface area gets larger from shapes where the volume gets larger too?
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.model.0: 1×1×20 is long and thin, so its surface area is 82 but its volume is 20, while 3×3×3 is close to a cube, with surface area 54 and volume 27. When a box is long and thin, there is a lot of outside but not much room inside.
x-m-e6-05.s.s2.because.model.1: Only one edge is very long and the others are 1, so the surface area gets bigger but the inside hardly grows. For example, 1×1×20 has a volume of 20 and 3×3×3 has 27.

x-m-e6-06.title: Fixing the surface area of a box with no lid
x-m-e6-06.topic: Volume and surface area of a rectangular prism
x-m-e6-06.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution for the surface area of a box with no lid, check by counting the faces, and correct it.
x-m-e6-06.material: You want to cover the outside of a rectangular box with no lid (the top is open), 6 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 5 cm high, with colored paper. Here is Harin's solution (area units are cm²).
x-m-e6-06.thinking.0: Find the error in the solution
x-m-e6-06.thinking.2: Fix the mistake and find the right answer
x-m-e6-06.prereq.0: The number of faces of a rectangular prism and the relationship between opposite faces
x-m-e6-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Harin's solution.
x-m-e6-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, compare the number of faces it mentions with the number you multiplied by in the calculation.
x-m-e6-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the explanation in each line and the expression match for how many faces of the same shape there are.
x-m-e6-06.s.s1.line.0: There is no lid, so we count without one top face.
x-m-e6-06.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. There are 2 side faces, but only the area of one face, 20, was used. It should be 20 × 2 = 40, so the surface area is 24 + 60 + 40 = 124 cm².
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose a good way to check that Harin's answer 104 is wrong.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.hint.0: First count how many faces the box is made of.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many faces were added once in the expression and compare.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.o.a: Decide that the answer 104 is right because it is a multiple of 4
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.r.a: Being a multiple of 4 has nothing to do with whether the answer is right. You need to check whether the solution counted the faces correctly.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.o.b: Count the faces that were used. A box with no lid has 5 faces
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.r.b: You checked the solution by matching it to the number of faces.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.o.c: Compare the volume (length × width × height) with the answer 104
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.r.c: Volume is a different quantity from surface area, and the units are different too. Comparing them can't tell you whether the surface area is right.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.o.d: Subtract the area of the top face from the surface area of a box with a lid and compare
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.r.d: You tried to check by comparing with a value found another way.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.explain: The faces used in Harin's expression are only 4: 1 bottom, 2 front and back, and 1 side. There should be 5, so you can tell one face is missing.
x-m-e6-06.s.s2.acc.0: Subtracting the top face 24 from the surface area 148 of a box with a lid gives 124, so you can tell 104 is wrong.
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.prompt: Write the correct surface area and explain what Harin missed.
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write the sum of the correct solution.
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.hint.1: Put into your words how many pairs of opposite faces there are.
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the sum you wrote the sum of all 5 faces?
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect how many side faces there are to the expression?
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.model.0: The side faces are 4×5=20 and there are two of them, so 40. So 24+60+40=124 cm².
x-m-e6-06.s.s3.model.1: The side faces also have 2 opposite faces, so it should be 20×2=40. The sum is 124 cm².

x-m-e6-07.title: To keep the strawberry milk taste the same when making more
x-m-e6-07.goal: Check with data that increasing amounts by adding the same number changes the taste, and fix your judgment with a proportion that keeps the ratio the same.
x-m-e6-07.material: Suyeon made strawberry milk syrup with 3 cups of strawberries and 2 cups of milk, and the taste was just right. She wants to make more with the same taste, and Suyeon thinks, “If I add 3 more cups of strawberries, I just add 3 more cups of milk.”
x-m-e6-07.thinking.0: Fix your first idea using new data
x-m-e6-07.thinking.1: Check whether the values of the ratios are equal
x-m-e6-07.prereq.0: The meaning of a ratio and the value of a ratio
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write the ratio of strawberries to milk in the same way and compare.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart at which step you thought “how many times as much” and at which step you thought “how many more cups.”
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.info: Using Suyeon's method, she made it with 6 cups of strawberries (3 cups added) and 5 cups of milk (3 cups added), and the milk taste was much stronger than the original.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you see this result?
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.after: 3:2 means strawberries are 1.5 times the milk, and 6:5 means 1.2 times, so the ratio changed. Adding the same number may not keep the ratio.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It was a coincidence, so try the same method once more
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: When a result looks strange, you can look at the method itself before blaming chance.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Check whether the ratio of strawberries to milk, 3:2, changed in 6:5
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You used the result as a clue for checking the method.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Add more milk to fix the taste
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The result already leans toward milk, so adding more milk takes it even further away.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.1.info: She doubled the strawberries (6 cups) and doubled the milk (4 cups), and the taste was the same as the original.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: To get the same taste with 9 cups of strawberries, how many cups of milk are needed?
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.1.after: The 3 cups of strawberries became 9 cups, 3 times as many, so the 2 cups of milk must also be 3 times as many, 6 cups. 3:2 = 9:6.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You made the strawberries 3 times as many, so you made the milk 3 times as many too. That is the idea of keeping the ratio 3:2.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The strawberries increased by 6 cups, so you increased the milk by 6 cups. You are using the first idea, “add the same number,” again.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You guessed something in the middle of strawberries and milk. You didn't check whether 3:2 is kept.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.2.info: This time she wants to use 4.5 cups of strawberries. Calling the amount of milk □ cups, she set up the proportion 3 : 2 = 4.5 : □.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose the right equation for finding □.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.2.after: In a proportion, the product of the outer two numbers equals the product of the inner two numbers. 3 × □ = 2 × 4.5, so □ = 3.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You swapped the outer terms and the inner terms when multiplying. Look again at which numbers are paired in the multiplication of a proportion.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The strawberries increased by 1.5 cups, so you added 1.5 cups to the milk too. You went back to the first idea.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You used the property that the product of the outer terms equals the product of the inner terms.
x-m-e6-07.s.s1.reflect: What was different between when you first thought “just add the same number” and when you set up the proportion at the end? What result made you change your mind?
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.prompt: Briefly tell Suyeon a way to make more with the same taste.
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.hint.0: Put into your words how many times as many strawberries you used.
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.hint.1: Give an example with a number made using your method.
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say the difference between the adding method and the multiplying method?
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: In your example, is the ratio really kept at 3:2?
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.model.0: If you double the strawberries, you have to double the milk too. Like 3:2 → 6:4.
x-m-e6-07.s.s2.model.1: You shouldn't add; you should multiply to keep the ratio the same. With 9 cups of strawberries, the milk is 6 cups.

x-m-e6-08.title: If the diameter doubles, does the area double?
x-m-e6-08.goal: Find the error in a solution and compare to check that when the diameter doubles, the area of a circle does not just double but gets even bigger, and explain why.
x-m-e6-08.material: At a pizza shop, a small pizza with a diameter of 10 cm costs 12000원 and a large pizza with a diameter of 20 cm costs 24000원. Yunho said, “The large pizza has twice the diameter and twice the price, so it's the same amount as 2 small pizzas.” Yuna wrote a solution to check (use 3.14 for pi; area units are cm²).
x-m-e6-08.thinking.0: Find the error in the solution
x-m-e6-08.thinking.2: Explain the relationship between radius and area
x-m-e6-08.prereq.0: The relationship between the radius and diameter of a circle
x-m-e6-08.prereq.1: Pi as 3.14 and how to find the area of a circle (Grade 6)
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Yuna's solution.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put the lines that find the areas of the two pizzas side by side and compare whether the number multiplied is the radius or the diameter.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.line.0: The radius of the small pizza is 5 cm and the radius of the large pizza is 10 cm.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.line.1: The area of the small pizza is 5 × 5 × 3.14 = 78.5.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.line.2: The area of the large pizza is 20 × 20 × 3.14 = 1256.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.line.3: 1256 ÷ 78.5 = 16, so the large pizza is 16 times the small pizza.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.line.4: So one large pizza is the same as 16 small pizzas.
x-m-e6-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first wrong place. In line 1 the radius of the large pizza was set as 10 cm, but in line 3 the diameter 20 was multiplied. 10 × 10 × 3.14 = 314 is correct. Lines 4 and 5 followed the wrong value in line 3.
x-m-e6-08.s.s2.prompt: Now that Yuna's solution is fixed, for 24000원, which gives more pizza: one large pizza or two small pizzas?
x-m-e6-08.s.s2.hint.0: Using the fixed values, find the area of one large pizza and one small pizza.
x-m-e6-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the total areas of the two ways to spend 24000원.
x-m-e6-08.s.s2.o.c: Two small pizzas give more. Because there are more pizzas
x-m-e6-08.s.s2.r.c: You only looked at the number of pizzas. You need to compare how different the size of each pizza is.
x-m-e6-08.s.s2.explain: One small pizza is 78.5 cm² and one large pizza is 314 cm², which is 4 times as much. Two small pizzas are 157 cm², so one large pizza gives more.
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.prompt: Explain why, when the diameter (radius) becomes 2 times as big, the area of a circle doesn't become 2 times as big but gets even bigger.
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.hint.0: Compare how the multiplication expression changed when the radius went from 5 to 10.
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.hint.1: Put into your words how many times the radius is multiplied.
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When the radius becomes 2 times as big, ...
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your reason include “the radius is multiplied twice”?
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you guess how many times as big the area would be if the diameter became 3 times as big?
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.model.0: When the radius becomes 2 times as big, the radius is multiplied twice, so the area becomes 2×2=4 times as big. 5×5×3.14=78.5 and 10×10×3.14=314.
x-m-e6-08.s.s3.model.1: If the diameter is 2 times as big, the radius is 2 times as big too, but the area is found by multiplying the radius twice (squaring it), so it becomes 4 times as big.

x-m-e6-09.title: The round path around the pond
x-m-e6-09.goal: Work backwards from the difference of the areas of two circles to find the radius values, and explain that the area can be the same even when the width of the path is different.
x-m-e6-09.material: In a park there is a circular pond, and a round path of constant width surrounds it. The area of the path is 75.36 m². The pond's radius r (m) and the path's outer radius R (m) are both whole numbers and at most 20 m (use 3.14 for pi).
x-m-e6-09.thinking.0: Write an expression using the difference of areas
x-m-e6-09.thinking.1: Find several solutions that meet the conditions
x-m-e6-09.thinking.2: Explain the relationship between width and area
x-m-e6-09.prereq.0: How to find the area of a circle (Grade 6)
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.prompt: Which expression correctly shows the area of the round path?
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.hint.0: Picture the whole circle including the path, and the pond circle.
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.hint.1: How can you show the area of the path alone using the areas of the two circles?
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.r.a: You used the width (R − r) like a radius. The path is the part left when you take the inner circle away from the outer circle.
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.r.b: You thought of subtracting the area of the pond from the area of the outer circle.
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.r.c: This is close to the formula for the circumference of a circle. For area, the radius is multiplied twice.
x-m-e6-09.s.s1.explain: Area of the path = area of the outer circle − area of the pond = 3.14 × R × R − 3.14 × r × r.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different (R, r) for which the area of the path is 75.36 m². Since there is a pond, r is at least 1.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.hint.0: To get rid of the 3.14 in the expression, what could you do to both sides?
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.hint.1: Change r one at a time and check what R×R − r×r has to be.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.ok.c1: R and r are whole numbers within the range.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.fail.c1: R must be a whole number at most 20 and r a whole number at least 1.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The outer radius R must be bigger than the pond radius r.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The area of the path is 75.36.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.fail.c3: The area of the path is not 75.36.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.explain: 75.36 ÷ 3.14 = 24, so you just need whole numbers with R×R − r×r = 24. 7×7 − 5×5 = 24 and 5×5 − 1×1 = 24. The widths are 2 m and 4 m, respectively.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.prompt: In the two solutions the width of the path is different but the area was the same. Explain why this is possible.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Find the widths (R − r) of the two solutions and compare.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Remember how many times the radius is multiplied when finding the area of a circle.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The area of a circle is ...
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you make another example where the widths are the same but the areas are not?
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the area grows differently for the inner path and the outer path?
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.model.0: The area is found by squaring the radius, so even with the same width, the area gets bigger the farther out you go. So different widths can give the same area.
x-m-e6-09.s.s2.because.model.1: The area of a circle is proportional to the radius multiplied twice, so even a narrow path (7−5=2 m) can have the same area as the inner path with a width of 4 m (5−1) if it is farther out, because the area is bigger there.
